stories.headline: U.S., Mexico, and Canada Announce Ebola Travel Screening Measures Ahead of 2026 World Cup
stories.summary:
The United States, Mexico, and Canada — the three co-hosts of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, which begins in June — announced coordinated public health travel measures Thursday targeting travelers arriving from parts of Africa with the highest Ebola risk. The move comes after the World Health Organization declared the Congo Ebola outbreak a public health emergency of international concern, with the case count having surpassed 900.

The screening protocols are designed to protect the millions of athletes, fans, and tourists expected to attend matches across dozens of host cities in all three countries. Officials did not specify the precise nature of every measure but described the approach as coordinated entry screening and monitoring for travelers from high-risk zones.

The World Cup presents a unique biosecurity challenge given the scale of international travel involved. Health authorities have pointed to the need to balance open borders for the tournament with precautions against importing a disease that has already strained the global response capacity in central Africa.

The announcement adds a new dimension to ongoing coverage of the Ebola outbreak, which has been marked by vaccine shortages and insufficient international funding. It also raises logistical questions for FIFA and national health ministries as they finalize tournament preparations.

stories.headline: Americans Spending Faster Than Income Grows as Iran War Energy Shock Strains Household Budgets
stories.summary:
New data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis released Thursday show that American consumers are spending at a rate that outpaces income growth, with households increasingly drawing down savings to sustain their purchasing. A key inflation gauge accelerated in April to its highest level in three years, compounding the financial pressure on families.

Economists attribute a significant portion of the strain to the energy price shock stemming from the U.S.-Iran conflict, which has driven up fuel and utility costs. Consumer spending has nominally held up, defying pessimistic sentiment surveys, but analysts warn the reliance on savings drawdowns is a fragile and unsustainable foundation for the broader economy.

The data carry substantial political weight, with midterm elections roughly five months away. Congressional Republicans and the White House face difficult messaging on the economy as inflation and energy costs erode the real purchasing power of voters who had been promised economic stability.

The report underscores how the military and foreign policy dimensions of the Iran conflict are producing domestic economic consequences that extend well beyond the defense sector, touching everyday household finances across income levels.

stories.headline: Australia Charges Woman Returned from Syria with Islamic State Membership
stories.summary:
Australian federal police announced Thursday that a 34-year-old woman who returned from Syria last year has been charged with membership in a terrorist organization and entering a declared conflict zone. The woman, identified in local media as Rayann El Houli, traveled to Syria in 2013 or 2014, was detained by Kurdish forces in 2019, and held in the al-Hawl camp before her return to Australia in September.

The charges carry a maximum penalty of up to 10 years in prison each. The announcement follows the recent return of two groups of women and children from the al-Roj detention camp in northeastern Syria, completing what authorities described as the last batch of Australians held there. Three other women who returned earlier this month also face charges including crimes against humanity and enslavement.

The cases have reignited a sharp political debate in Australia. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has taken a hard line, stating that those who chose to go must face consequences, while advocates for the returning women and children argue Australia has a legal obligation to repatriate its citizens and that children should not be held responsible for their parents' decisions.

Federal police assistant commissioner Hilda Sirec warned that the absence of charges against other returning women should not be interpreted as the end of investigations, saying all adult women who had recently arrived were still under active review.

stories.headline: Michigan Gov. Whitmer Rules Out 2028 Presidential Run
stories.summary:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced Thursday that she will not seek the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, ending months of speculation about her potential candidacy. Speaking in an interview with Fox 2 Detroit during the annual Mackinac policy conference, Whitmer said plainly: "I think there will be a robust group of people running for president. I will not be one of them in 2028."

Whitmer, 54, had long been regarded by Democratic strategists as a high-value potential candidate given her two decisive victories in Michigan, a battleground state that President Trump carried in both the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections. She is set to leave the governor's office at the end of this year due to term limits.

Her withdrawal narrows one of the more prominent potential lanes in what is shaping up to be a wide-open Democratic primary. The Mackinac conference has become a venue of presidential speculation this week, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin — both considered potential 2028 contenders — also in attendance.

Whitmer had previously kept her options open, saying in April that she was "not sure" whether she would put her name on a ballot again but had "a lot of gas in the tank." Her statement Thursday represents the clearest and most definitive answer she has given on the question.

stories.headline: DOJ Opens Criminal Investigation Into Trump Accuser E. Jean Carroll for Alleged Perjury
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice has opened a criminal investigation into writer E. Jean Carroll, who successfully sued President Trump twice for sexual assault and defamation, examining whether she committed perjury in connection with those civil cases. The investigation, led by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois, centers on whether Carroll lied during a 2022 deposition when she stated she received no outside funding for her lawsuit — a claim later contradicted when court filings revealed LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman had helped cover some of her legal fees and expenses.

Carroll won two civil verdicts against Trump: a 2023 jury found him liable for sexual assault and defamation, ordering him to pay $5 million, and a 2024 jury found him liable for defamation again, awarding Carroll $83 million. Both judgments have been upheld on appeal, though Trump has petitioned the Supreme Court to overturn the first. A federal appeals court previously ruled that Carroll had "plausibly represented" she had forgotten about the limited outside funding, and that she was not personally involved in managing her litigation costs.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who personally represented Trump during the Carroll appeal cases, is recused from the investigation. Trump has repeatedly called on the DOJ since returning to office to prosecute political adversaries, and the DOJ recently created a $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund that drew bipartisan criticism. Carroll's attorney had not responded to requests for comment at the time of reporting.

Critics and legal observers argue the investigation represents an escalation of the administration's use of the Justice Department against Trump's opponents, while supporters contend the perjury allegation — if substantiated — warrants investigation regardless of the political context. The DOJ declined to comment on the probe.

stories.headline: Update: Congo Ebola Epidemic Outpacing Global Response as Vaccines and Medicines Remain Unavailable
stories.summary:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, is spreading at a pace that exceeds the international response by weeks if not months, according to Reuters and the WHO. The Bundibugyo variant has no approved medicines or vaccines, leaving health workers with fewer tools than in previous outbreaks, while active armed conflict in affected regions is further hampering containment efforts.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said fighting in eastern DRC was directly blocking outbreak response, leaving thousands of potentially exposed individuals unreached. Some countries in the region have begun taking precautionary measures that diverge from WHO guidance, reflecting growing fears about cross-border spread into East Africa.

The outbreak has now surpassed 900 confirmed and suspected cases, with the death toll exceeding 220, figures that represent some of the most acute Ebola numbers in recent memory outside of the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic. A significant funding gap in the international response has been flagged by health authorities as a critical obstacle to scaling up operations.

The combination of an untreatable strain, active conflict, and an underfunded response has led health officials to warn of potential catastrophic spread if the situation is not urgently addressed. The outbreak has drawn comparisons to past episodes where delayed global action allowed Ebola to spiral beyond initial containment zones.

stories.headline: Australia Files $1.4 Billion Lawsuit Against 3M Over PFAS Contamination at Military Bases
stories.summary:
The Australian government has launched the largest legal claim in the country's history, suing U.S. manufacturing conglomerate 3M for AU$2 billion (approximately US$1.4 billion) over contamination of 28 defence sites with per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS or "forever chemicals," found in firefighting foam the company supplied to the military. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland announced the action Thursday, stating the government has already spent more than AU$1 billion investigating and remediating affected sites and seeks to recover those costs from 3M.

The lawsuit alleges 3M withheld and misrepresented information about the environmental and health risks of its aqueous film-forming foam, giving assurances of safety it knew to be inconsistent with its own internal findings. PFAS compounds do not break down under normal environmental conditions and have been linked to cancer and other serious health conditions; 3M announced in 2022 it would stop producing them.

3M denied primary liability, stating it has never manufactured PFAS in Australia and ceased selling the firefighting foam there 20 years ago. The company also noted that Australia's Department of Defence continued using the PFAS-containing foam for two decades after 3M stopped selling it in the country, and said it would defend itself through the legal process.

The case adds to a global wave of litigation against 3M over PFAS contamination; the company reached an $10.3 billion settlement with U.S. water utilities in 2023. Australia's action is notable for being government-initiated and for its scale, signaling increased willingness by national governments to pursue major American corporations over chemical contamination of public assets.

stories.headline: Former Red Army Faction Member Sentenced to 13 Years After Three Decades as a Fugitive
stories.summary:
A German court on Wednesday sentenced Daniela Klette, 67, to 13 years in prison for a series of armed robberies carried out between 1999 and 2016, concluding a case against one of Europe's most wanted fugitives. Klette, a former member of the far-left Red Army Faction — also known as the Baader-Meinhof gang — had evaded capture for more than 30 years before being arrested in Berlin in February 2024 after an investigative journalist identified her using AI-powered facial recognition software.

The court in Verden, Lower Saxony, found Klette guilty of aggravated robbery, weapons violations, and other offenses in connection with eight raids on supermarkets and armored cash transport vehicles across northern and western Germany. The final robbery in 2016 netted nearly €1.4 million. Two alleged accomplices and former RAF members, Burkhard Garweg and Ernst-Volker Staub, remain at large.

Klette had been living under a false identity in Berlin's Kreuzberg neighborhood, walking her dog and greeting neighbors who described her as friendly and unremarkable. A search of her apartment uncovered weapons, ammunition, a replica rocket-propelled grenade, wigs, false identification documents, gold, and €240,000 in cash. Her defense had sought acquittal, and dozens of supporters in the courtroom booed the verdict, chanting "freedom for Daniela."

The RAF conducted bombings, assassinations, and kidnappings from the early 1970s through the early 1990s before disbanding. Due to statutes of limitations, Klette cannot be tried for terrorism-related offenses from that era, though federal prosecutors may pursue a separate trial over alleged complicity in three specific RAF attacks. The case drew widespread attention in Germany for both its Cold War-era political dimensions and the role of AI technology in finally securing her capture.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Military Shoots Down Iranian Drones, Strikes Ground Station Near Bandar Abbas
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command forces shot down four Iranian one-way attack drones threatening the Strait of Hormuz area on Wednesday and struck an Iranian ground control station in Bandar Abbas that was preparing to launch a fifth drone, according to U.S. officials speaking anonymously. The strikes represent the latest exchange of fire in a conflict now nearly three months old. President Trump, speaking at a Cabinet meeting Wednesday, said Iran is "negotiating on fumes" and insisted that November's midterm elections would not pressure him into rushing a deal.

The emerging diplomatic framework would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and provide Trump with grounds to claim Iran's nuclear capability has been diminished, but significant issues remain unresolved. Trump also suggested the U.S. might withhold a final deal unless more Gulf nations join the Abraham Accords, saying some countries "owe that to us" and should normalize ties with Israel. Nuclear analysts have identified potential third-party custodians for Iran's enriched uranium as part of a possible agreement.

The ongoing conflict has drawn fierce criticism from Republican hawks who argue the emerging terms are too lenient on Iran's leadership. Trump faces pressure from multiple directions — allies pressing for a deal, hardliners demanding more concessions from Tehran, and a domestic political audience wary of a prolonged military engagement. The situation remains fluid as U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks in Qatar.

stories.headline: Federal Judge Clears Trump Mail-In Ballot Executive Order to Proceed
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., declined Thursday to temporarily block President Trump's March executive order imposing new restrictions on mail-in voting, allowing it to stand while legal challenges from Democratic groups continue through the courts. The order directs the federal government to establish a list of eligible voters based on available citizenship data and instructs the U.S. Postal Service to implement new verification procedures. A separate ruling from another federal judge on the same order is expected soon.

Democrats and voting-rights advocates have argued the executive order unconstitutionally infringes on states' authority to run their own elections and could disenfranchise millions of eligible voters who rely on mail-in ballots, particularly elderly, disabled, and military voters. Supporters of the order contend it is a necessary safeguard against non-citizen voting and election fraud, and that the president has the authority to direct federal agencies to verify voter eligibility.

The ruling is the latest front in a broader legal and political battle over voting rules ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections. Because multiple courts are weighing challenges simultaneously, the legal status of the order could change quickly. The outcome carries national significance, as mail-in voting expanded substantially during the 2020 and 2022 election cycles.

stories.headline: Jill Biden Says She Feared Joe Biden Was Having a Stroke During 2024 Presidential Debate
stories.summary:
Former First Lady Jill Biden revealed in a forthcoming CBS News interview that she believed her husband, President Joe Biden, was having a stroke as she watched his June 2024 debate performance against Donald Trump. "I was frightened, because I had never ever seen Joe like that before or since. Never," she told CBS News's Rita Braver. "As I watched it, I thought, 'Oh, my God, he's having a stroke.' And it scared me to death."

The admission is notable because Jill Biden publicly praised her husband's debate performance at the time, telling a post-debate rally crowd in Atlanta that he "did such a great job" and "answered every question." Biden's team had attributed his raspy voice and halting delivery to illness. The former president ultimately withdrew from the 2024 race weeks later, endorsing Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in November.

The interview adds to a growing body of post-election accounts about the state of Biden's health and the deliberations inside his inner circle. Critics, including many Republicans and some Democrats, have long argued that the former president's condition was concealed from the public during his time in office. Supporters have maintained Biden remained capable of performing his duties throughout his term. The CBS News interview is scheduled to air Sunday.

stories.headline: EU Fines Chinese Retailer Temu €200 Million for Allowing Illegal Products on Platform
stories.summary:
The European Commission imposed a €200 million ($232 million) fine on Chinese-owned online retailer Temu on Thursday for failing to prevent the sale of illegal and dangerous products, including baby toys with hazardous chemicals and chargers that failed basic electrical safety tests. The penalty is only the second ever issued under the EU's Digital Services Act, following a €120 million fine against Elon Musk's X social media network in December. EU tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen said the decision was intended to send a "very strong message" to the platform.

An independent investigation, including mystery shopping exercises, found that a high percentage of chargers sold through Temu failed electrical safety tests and that many baby toys contained chemicals above legal limits or featured small detachable parts posing suffocation hazards. In addition to paying the fine, Temu must submit an action plan by August 28 outlining how it will address the failures; the Commission then has two months to evaluate compliance.

Temu said it disagreed with the ruling and considered the fine disproportionate, noting the investigation covered 2024 and did not reflect its current systems. The company said it was reviewing the decision and considering all available options. The case underscores increasing regulatory scrutiny of Chinese e-commerce platforms operating in Western markets, particularly regarding product safety standards.

stories.headline: Update: White House Calls Iranian Draft Agreement a 'Complete Fabrication' as Ceasefire Strains
stories.summary:
The White House sharply rejected a draft memorandum of understanding published by Iranian state media Wednesday, calling it a "complete fabrication" — the latest flashpoint in fragile U.S.-Iran peace negotiations. The rejection came as President Trump told a Cabinet meeting he believes Iran is trying to run out the clock until November midterm elections, declaring Iranian leaders had "miscalculated" if they thought domestic politics would force him into a rushed deal.

The diplomatic turbulence coincided with fresh military skirmishes. The U.S. military shot down four Iranian one-way attack drones in the Strait of Hormuz and struck an Iranian ground control station near Bandar Abbas that was preparing to launch a fifth drone, a U.S. official told reporters. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed in response that they had targeted an American military base, calling the U.S. strikes a "blatant violation" of the ceasefire and international law. Oil prices rose sharply on the renewed hostilities.

Trump struck an ambiguous tone at the Cabinet meeting, at times hardening U.S. positions and at others appearing to soften them, while warning he may have to "finish the job" militarily if no deal is reached soon. He also threatened to "blow up" Oman after reports that Tehran and Muscat were discussing jointly charging a toll for ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, which has been largely closed since the war began in late February.

The breakdown in diplomatic signaling is significant: the U.S. and Iran had appeared on the verge of de-escalation before this week's exchange of strikes. Kuwait reported responding to missile and drone threats of its own, underscoring the regional spillover risk. Separately, the Pentagon warned allies it plans to reduce U.S. NATO contributions by up to half amid the ongoing Iran conflict, and Ukrainian President Zelensky wrote to Trump urging the U.S. to supply Patriot interceptors as the Iran war drains shared missile-defense stockpiles.

stories.headline: Sixteen Girls Killed in Fire at Kenyan Boarding School
stories.summary:
A fire broke out in the early hours of Thursday at Utumishi Girls Academy, a boarding school in Gilgil, Kenya, approximately 120 kilometers northwest of Nairobi, killing at least 16 students and injuring dozens more. The blaze began around 1:00 a.m. local time and engulfed a dormitory housing roughly 220 students while they slept, completely destroying the building's first floor before firefighters extinguished it by 3:00 a.m.

Kenya's Education Minister Julius Ogamba and Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen both traveled to the scene, where anxious parents gathered seeking news of their children. Officials said 71 students were treated and discharged from hospital, while seven remained admitted. Some students fled into surrounding areas during the chaos and police were still searching for them at the time of reporting.

Authorities have cordoned off the school and opened an investigation into the cause. Kenya has experienced a series of deadly school fires in recent years, some caused by arson from disgruntled students and others by accident, with overcrowded dormitories and blocked fire exits frequently cited as factors amplifying casualties.

stories.headline: Former CIA Official Arrested After FBI Finds $40 Million in Gold Bars at Virginia Home
stories.summary:
Federal authorities have arrested a former senior U.S. government official after FBI agents executing a search warrant at his Virginia home discovered approximately 303 one-kilogram gold bars valued at more than $40 million, along with roughly $2 million in cash and 35 luxury watches. David Rush, identified by the New York Times as a recently retired senior CIA official who held top-secret clearance, has been charged with criminal theft of public money.

Court documents state that between November 2025 and March 2026, Rush made multiple requests to the U.S. government to receive large quantities of foreign currency and gold bars for purported "work-related expenses," which were granted. The CIA subsequently could not locate the gold or significant amounts of the foreign currency, nor any record of Rush accounting for them. CIA Director John Ratcliffe referred the matter to the FBI after an internal investigation identified potential violations of law.

Rush is also accused of lying about his educational background and military service during the government hiring process, and of fraudulently collecting thousands of dollars in military leave pay. He was arrested on May 19 and is being held pending a hearing. His attorney declined to comment. Court documents do not specify why Rush kept the assets at his residence.

stories.headline: Update: Israel Orders 17% of Lebanese Territory Evacuated, Strikes 100 Hezbollah Sites
stories.summary:
The Israeli military issued an evacuation order Thursday covering approximately 17 percent of Lebanese territory, the first such order since a ceasefire took effect on April 17, as hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah intensified sharply in the country's south. The Israeli Defense Forces simultaneously announced it had struck more than 100 Hezbollah infrastructure sites and fighters, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to "crush" the Iran-backed group.

The Israeli strikes occurred while Iranian and Qatari negotiators were in Doha for U.S.-Iran peace talks, adding pressure to already strained ceasefire arrangements across the region. Clashes between Israel and Hezbollah have been escalating near the Litani River in southern Lebanon, and few in Lebanon believe ongoing diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran will deliver peace to their country.

The widening Israeli offensive comes as Iran simultaneously engages in conflict with U.S. forces and negotiations in Qatar, stretching diplomatic and military dynamics across multiple fronts simultaneously. The BBC reported that Israel has also been expanding strikes into eastern Lebanon, and its warplanes have moved further inland after months of focusing primarily on southern Lebanon.
